chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . chunks.citation: Badawi, AK et al. (2022). Advanced wastewater treatment process using algal photo-bioreactor associated with dissolved-air flotation system: A pilot-scale demonstration. J WATER PROCESS ENG.
chunks.text: Within the framework of this study, an algal photo-bioreactor combined with a dissolved air flotation system (DAF) was used for the removal of COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP from primary treated wastewater. The optimum operating conditions for the algal photo-bioreactor were determined through batch experiments, which are pH 7, temperature 25 • C, light intensity 90 μmol m − 2 S − 1 and mixing rate 100 rpm. Those optimal conditions were used in a scaled-up pilot plant treatment system to treat primary treated wastewater from ZENIN WWTP-Egypt. The operation has shown significant results where COD, BOD 5 , TSS, TN and TP have been removal with efficiencies of 56.4%, 61%, 59.2%, 48.3% and 51.7% respectively. These findings have been compared with previous studies. These findings proved the efficacy of algal-bacterial integrated treatment systems combined with DAF as a wastewater treatment technology that does not require any additional tertiary treatment to release the effluent to sewer systems.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: The system of hydraulically connected WRRFs presented in this study is modeled after the interconnected system of wastewater conveyance and treatment facilities known as the Joint Outfall System (JOS), which is managed and maintained by the Los Angeles County Sanitation District (LACSD). The JOS provides wastewater treatment services for 4.8 million residents in 73 cities. Designed to take advantage of the regional topography, the JOS conveys the collected wastewater to 7 satellite and 1 centralized WRRF mainly by gravity (See Fig. 1 ). The satellite facilities provide the dual purpose of hydraulically relieving the downstream centralized system and of supplying an alternative water resource to the local communities. Each of the satellite WRRFs can be categorized as an extraction type because the wastewater is directly mined out of the sewer system. The harvested wastewater is subsequently treated to title 22 standards via a treatment train comprising primary sedimentation, activated sludge treatment, coagulation, filtration, chlorination, and de-chlorination. The residual solids produced on-site are discharged in the main trunk sewers of the JOS from which they are transported downstream and treated at the centralized wastewater treatment facility.

chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.
